Team: 5th Grade Science - The Wilson School
Team #: 19240
Plant the Moon, Jr., Fall 2024
Elementary Level
QUESTION: 
How do different lighting colors affect spinach 
growth in Martian regolith, Missouri soil, and 
Charlie’s compost?
BACKGROUND:
Spinach 
Spinach is good for you and an important crop to 
grow on Mars. It has a lot of benefits. Spinach is 
high in nutrients, like vitamins A, C, E, and K, iron, folate, magnesium, and even protein. (Eating 
Well) Spinach can help support immune function. It will aid the digestive system and may even have 
anticancer properties. (Medical News Today) 
Spinach is very nutritious for anyone to eat, and it is important to have good nutrition for anyone 
traveling to Mars. The proteins inside spinach can help astronauts get protein on Mars. Spinach can 
sometimes lower your blood pressure and help your skin become smoother and healthier. (WebMD) 
These effects can help astronauts with any problems like getting sick or getting cancer and they can 
help with stomach aches. This plant is great to grow on Mars! 
Spinach grows most quickly in well-drained soil rich in organic matter such as compost or composted 
manure and with a pH of 6.5 to 7. A pH describes the acidity or alkalinity of your soil or other things. 
A pH ranges from 0-14, 7 being a neutral factor. (Bonnie’s Plants) We will be trying to keep our pH 
close to neutral.
Missouri Soil 
Missouri soil consists of a combination of sand, silt, and clay particles (Mefro: Missouri State Soil). 
Clay soil can hold water and nutrients very well. Clay particles hold onto ammonium and trace 
elements like potassium, calcium, and magnesium. Fertile soil is a result. Clay can be hard to work 
with, but breaking it up helps water and airflow in it. Also, adding organic matter, like manure can 
help it. (University of Missouri)
We took soil from our schoolyard. We made sure we took the soil and not the mulch on top of it. 
Once we took our sample, we did a mason jar test and discovered our soil is 100% clay. (Mason Jar 
Test)

Charlie’s Compost
We are adding compost to our Missouri soil. This is a soil amendment. A soil amendment is a 
product that is added to soil to improve it. It is made of organic matter and it helps improve the 
texture and structure of the soil by adding nutrients, improving drainage or water retention, and 
adjusting the pH level. (Ted’s Gardens)
We selected a compost product from Charlie’s Compost. It is made in Kentucky and certified 
organic. We liked what their website said, “It is concentrated plant fertilizer that will jumpstart the 
bioactivity and nutrient content of your soil. If you want beautiful, healthy, and vibrant plants or 
vegetables, this is the product for you!” The website also says it adds nutrients along with 
microorganisms and matter that are very important for soil health. The ingredients are from chicken 
manure and are composted cornstalks, composted wheat straw, composted forest products, 
composted fescue hay, clay, ACS N-converter, ACS Humifier, and ACS Finisher. (Charlie’s Compost)
The ratio recommended is 1 part compost to 4 parts soil. To use this, we will be putting 40 g of 
compost with 120 g of Missouri soil in each pot.
Martian Regolith
Martian regolith is the soil of Mars. It is made up of mineral matter and does not have organic 
materials like soil does on Earth. This is because organic material is made of biotic factors and since 
there is no life on Mars, organic material as we know it does not exist. Weathered volcanic rock 
makes up the mineral matter. It is mostly made of sand but also has some clay and silt particles. It is 
a reddish color from the iron oxide in it. We have information on the soil of Mars from rovers sent 
there. However, no regolith from Mars has come to Earth. Therefore, we are using a regolith simulant 
made by scientists to mimic the soil from Mars. (The Soil on Mars) (Martian Soil)
For our project, we are going to use 240 grams of Martian regolith, which will be 60% of our soil. We 
are hoping that the Missouri clay will help balance out the sandy nature of the regolith and that the 
compost will add the needed nutrients for plants to grow.

Lighting Color Effects on Plants
Plants react differently to different colored lights. 
Light causes plants to make their own energy (food) 
called photosynthesis. Studies have shown that green 
light is the least helpful in growing plants. This is 
because it is mostly reflected off the green plant. 
Blue light is helpful in the plant’s germination phase. 
This will help with the plant sprouting and 
developing roots. It also helps vegetative leaf 
growth. Violet or purple light has been shown to be 
good for helping the growth and development of 
leaves. Red light helps in the blooming and flowering 
phases. It has a long wavelength that allows it to 
radiate more energy and heat than other colors. 
(Lighting Spectrum for Plant Growth) (Can Colored Lights Help Plants Grow) (MDPI) 
For our project, we will use the following lights: red, blue, purple, and white. 
Why Are We Interested in This Topic?
We picked this topic because we think that the lighting might affect the plants in different ways than 
water and soil alone. We picked red, blue, violet, and white for our light colors. We also think that 
this topic is interesting because lighting is cool and fun to study. We love this project because we 
get to help astronauts figure out how to grow plants in space with Martian regolith. We are very 
excited because we get to use a replica of Martian soil. It helps us learn how to do things in space 
while staying on Earth. Plus it has been fun to collect soil and mix the compost, soil, and Martian 
regolith together. 
PROJECT HYPOTHESIS:
Based on our research, we think that blue light will produce the most growth since it is the most 
helpful in germination and helps encourage vegetative leaf growth.
INDEPENDENT VARIABLE: 
Our independent variable is what we are changing in this experiment. We are changing the color of 
the lighting used to grow the plants. Our colors are purple, red, blue, and white. We are testing two 
pots per color.
DEPENDENT VARIABLES:
The dependent variables are everything we are measuring. Our dependent variables in this 
experiment are the height the spinach grows, in centimeters, and the number of leaves sprouted on 
each plant.

CONTROLS:
The controls are what we keep constant. Here is how we will keep things the same:
●​ Plants are in the same location in the classroom.
●​ All pots will get a mixture of 40% soil + compost and 60% Martian regolith. Each pot will get 
120 g of Missouri soil mixed with 40 g of Charlie’s compost and 240 g of Martian regolith.
●​ The pots are all the same material and size. 
●​ All pots will get one spinach seed from the same package.
●​ We will water the plants at the same time and from the same water source. We will measure 
based on the reading from the moisture reader. We will not add water if moisture is at a 7 or 
higher. If the level is 4-6, we will add 10 mL of water. If the level is 0-3, we will add 20 mL of 
water.
●​ All plants are placed in the same type of greenhouse. This will help us keep temperature and 
humidity levels consistent. A thermometer is placed in each greenhouse to help us monitor 
temperature. 
●​ We will monitor the pH levels and consistently make adjustments based on the reading.
●​ Lighting was purchased from the same manufacturer. This is so they will have the same 
intensity and brightness. We will have the lights on at the same time and for the same length 
of time - 12 hours on and 12 hours off. We will make sure the angle and height are the same 
for each plant. The white light serves as our control since most plants get white light that 
imitates sunlight and allows us to compare colors.
●​ All plants will grow in the 8 week window given by PTMC.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN AND PROCEDURE:
1.​ Mix 60% Martian regolith (240 g) with 40% soil (40 g compost and 120 g Missouri clay soil).
2.​ Fill a pot with this mixture (400 g).
3.​ Repeat 7 more times, so you have 8 pots total. 
4.​ Place 2 pots in each of the 4 greenhouses. 
5.​ Put a grow light in each greenhouse. One will be set to white, one to red, one to blue, and 
one to violet. 
6.​ Set the timer so the greenhouse will have light for 12 hours daily. 
7.​ Label each plant. White light plants will be labeled as W1 & W2. Red light plants will be 
labeled as R1 & R2. Blue light plants will be labeled B1 & B2. Violet light plants will be labeled 
V1 & V2.
8.​ Plant one spinach seed in each pot 2.5 cm deep.
9.​ Each day, check the moisture level, pH, temperature, growth, and leaf count.
DATA, RESULTS, & ANALYSIS:
As our plants grew, we collected data on growth, leaf number, moisture level, and pH level. In 
looking at our data on growth height and leaf count, our hypothesis was inconclusive. There was not 
enough evidence to support it since the initial spinach crops that we planted all died and we had to 
replant. The new growth period had different results and we had to stop it at the end of the growth 
period, so it was hard to tell if the hypothesis was completely right or wrong. 
We realized that the most probable cause for our plants suddenly dying was bolting. Bolting is a 
process in which plants undergo too much stress and fall over and die. All of our plants did this. The 
stress may be caused by temperature, soil moisture, and too much light. (Houzz Q & A) This stress on 
the plants is caused by warm temperatures and spinach plants are happiest in colder climates closer 
to 4.4 - 21° Celsius. Spinach must have the correct amount of water. Our research told us to make

sure the soil did not get too dry. Additionally, longer daylight can cause bolting. (The Beginner’s 
Garden)
In response to our research on why our plants died, we made the following changes on November 4, 
the start of our 6th week of the growing season:
●​ Added 40 g of Charle’s compost to our pots. This now makes our pots 240 g regolith, 200 g 
of compost/soil. Our new per percentages is 220g/440g = 45% soil/compost and 240g/440g 
= 55% regolith. We wanted to make sure the plants had enough nutrients. 
●​ Replanted spinach in all the pots, 2.5 cm deep. We kept this the same from the first plant.
●​ Reset our light to 8 hours on daily instead of 12 hours. This is because we learned that longer 
daylight can cause bolting.
●​ We went to what we thought was the coolest place in the school to take temperature 
readings. It is consistent with our classroom at around 23 degrees C. Unfortunately, we do not 
think we can cool this down more and hope that the 2 degrees higher from the ideal 
temperature is not a big problem.
●​ Will be misting 3 sprays of water in all the pots each school day, regardless of the moisture 
level. This is because we often noticed the soil looking dry on top even when the moisture 
reader was telling us that it had enough water. This is also our plan to help cool them.

Our spinach plants in the white light were our control group. Both plants started to grow successfully 
but then died. Both also grew in our second planting. W1 sprouted on day 12 and W2 sprouted on 
day 11. W1 reached a maximum height of 5.2 cm and W2 reached 3 cm. Regarding leaf growth, W1 
produced 3 leaves, the most out of any plant. However, W1 in the replant produced 2 leaves and W2 
produced 2 leaves both times. In our first plant, W1 was alive for 22 days and W2 had 9 days. 22 
days alive was the longest amount of time any of our plants lived. Both were alive at the end of our 
growing period.
Even though W1 was only the second tallest plant in the experiment, the plants in the white light 
produced the most consistent growth. We replanted it took longer to sprout. We wished we had 
more time because we would like to see how much it could have grown.

For our first planting, our spinach plants in the blue light did not grow. After we replanted, B1 
started to grow on November 15. On November 19, B2 started to grow. They were consistent on 
growing and both ended on a height of 4 cm on the last day of the growing period. They both had 2 
leaves. We believe that the changing of the soil helped them regrow very well. The growth of 4 
centimeters in 5 days and 4 days respectively make our hypothesis look like it could be correct. 
However, with no growth in the first period, we are not sure.

Our spinach plants in the red light started off strong and then died in our first planting. In our second 
plant, R1 grew impressively well because it only took 3 days to sprout and when it did, it sprouted 
just as high (5 cm) as in our first growth period. R2 sprouted on day 12 and died. R2 reached a 
maximum height of 5.5 cm. R2 was the tallest plant in our study. But, it did not grow in the second 
growth period. When the plants in the red light grew, they all got 2 leaves. 
The red light plants make us wonder why there was good growth in the first planting period and 
impressive growth in it taking only 3 days to grow from 0-5 cm during the replant, but only for one 
plant. Our data may indicate that red light is better for the plants than the blue light, but we need 
more information and time to be sure, especially since R2 never grew.

Our spinach plants in the violet light were the least successful plants. Only V2 grew, and its 
maximum height was 3 cm. V2 sprouted on day 8 and died on day 20. It only grew for 17 days. After 
we replanted, V2 did not sprout again. V1 never grew. We do not think violet light is the best light 
for growing spinach plants.

Moisture, Temperature, and pH level
The temperature of the plants was pretty 
consistent. But sometimes out of the blue, the 
temperature would shoot up or shoot down. 
We noticed that V2 and V1 got up to the 
highest at 28°C. The lowest the temperature 
got was with our W2 plant at 20° C. The 
average temperature was between 22° to 23° 
C.
We also noticed that the moisture levels varied a 
lot. The most common level was 6 at the 
beginning and 10 at the end. We think that the 
plants sometimes got WAY over-watered at the 
end. Or that the moisture would sink to the 
bottom and not drain. And since our 
measurements were taken with the meter deep in 
the soil, this would cause the plants to not get 
enough moisture closer to the top of the soil. So, 
when we replanted, we added 3 sprays to help 
keep the topsoil from drying out.

The PH level was all the same the whole time. It stayed at 7. 
This is good because it means the soil stayed neutral. 
However, sometimes students would argue if it was 6.5. Our 
teacher taught us about precision of instruments, so we were 
told to round to the nearest whole number because our 
instrument only has whole numbers and not halves. 
FUTURE CONSIDERATIONS:
We would like to attempt this experiment again. We found 
that we were looking successful in our replant and would like 
to be able to confirm that. We were not able to finish our 
experiment since we ran out of time in this challenge. We 
really want to see what would happen if we had more time for 
our second replant. 
Since our replant looked like it produced better results, we 
will use the same soil composition for the pots as we did in 
our second growth period. We will also keep adding sprays of water to the top soil as we water. We 
will keep 8 hours of lighting instead of 12 hours. And, we will be more consistent in making 
measurements and observations. We think we can be better at that in the second try because we 
have more experience. 
CONCLUSIONS:
Our hypothesis was that we think that blue light will produce the most growth since it is the most 
helpful in germination and helps encourage vegetative leaf growth.
Our experiment did not give us the information to confirm or disprove our hypothesis. Our plants 
died and so we replanted. With a change in the nurtirents to the soil, we saw stronger growth but 
ran out of time. The results we did get in this shortened growing time showed promise to give us 
results that may be able to support or disprove our hypothesis. 
According to our data, blue light showed improvement in the replant. It grew quickly and stayed 
alive. It reached 4 cm in both plants in 4 and 5 days. In red, we found it also quickly grew to 5 cm in 
3 days, but only in one plant. For white, it was consistent. It had the longest time alive and all our 
plants grew. Violet was the most inconsistent. Only one plant grew out of the 4. It is difficult to say 
which light is for sure the best for growing spinach on Mars.
